title: What koans are not
hookLine: not riddles with clever answers; Soto Zen stresses just sitting instead, and both are Zen

cards: After two weeks of dogs, bowls, foxes, fingers, flags, flowers, faces, cats, good days and one hand, you might think Zen is basically koans. Step into a Soto Zen hall in Japan and there's something different.
People sitting facing a plain wall. No question to hold. No interview bell.
Just sitting, for a long time, very still. That's Zen too. Today the koans close with what they aren't, and with the other great way Zen is practiced.

teach.b: First, what koans are not. They're not riddles with clever answers; the teacher's bell sends clever answers back. They're not nonsense meant to confuse you; each grew out of a real encounter and points somewhere.
And they're not the only way to practice Zen. In Japan the two main Zen schools are Rinzai, which you've been meeting, and Soto.
Soto was brought from China by a Japanese monk named Dogen.

His teacher in China had a phrase for the heart of practice: just sitting. In Japanese, shikantaza. You sit upright, usually facing a wall, eyes half open, and you don't hold a koan, count breaths or aim at anything.
You just sit, fully awake to sitting. Remember nothing to attain, from the Heart Sutra: Dogen taught that sitting isn't a means to awakening later. Sitting is awakening, being expressed.
The difference isn't new. In Song-dynasty China, Dahui championed working on a single koan phrase, while Hongzhi taught a quiet practice he called silent illumination.
They disagreed, and were friends: tradition says Hongzhi asked Dahui to handle his funeral.
Today Rinzai teachers stress koans, Soto teachers stress just sitting, and both schools say the other is Zen. Soto teachers study koans too; Dogen wrote about them often.
And some lineages, especially in the West, teach both.

Two weeks of koans, closed in silence: don't solve it, mu, wash your bowl, not blind to cause, your own finger, mind moves, the smile, before you were born, sandals on the head, every day is a good day, ordinary mind, one hand, carry it.

how: In Soto Zen, practitioners sit shikantaza, usually facing a wall, without a koan; in Rinzai Zen they usually sit facing into the room and work with koans. Some lineages teach both.

o: the Soto name for working on a koan phrase
focused breathing to reach a calm, still mind
just sitting, holding no koan and aiming at nothing

games.q: match each name to the way of practice.
p: just sitting, often facing a wall
worked on a single koan phrase

s: koans are nonsense meant to confuse
each grew from a real encounter and points somewhere.
Soto Zen was brought to Japan by Dogen
his Chinese teacher's phrase was 'just sitting'.
Dogen wrote about them often; Soto simply centers practice on just sitting.

games.q: two friends argue: one sits with koans, one just sits facing a wall. which one is doing Zen?
o: only the one facing the wall.
both; Rinzai and Soto each recognize the other as Zen.
games.why: the two schools stress different practices and have for centuries, and both call the other Zen.

practice: No koan, no counting, no word on the breath: sit upright as if a thread were lifting the crown of your head, eyes resting half open on the floor or a wall a little in front of you.
When thoughts come, don't follow them and don't push them away; let them pass like weather. Just this body, sitting, breathing.

wordCard.voice: Shikantaza. Just sitting, facing a wall, holding no koan and aiming at nothing: the other great way Zen is practiced.

orig.note: Japanese shikantaza: 'nothing but sitting', the phrase Dogen took from his teacher Rujing.

carryVoice: Your line: just sitting. Nothing to solve, nothing to add. That's two weeks of koans, closed.

sources.ref: Dahui Zonggao and Hongzhi Zhengjue, letters and records
